lesson.text: Quick memory: in 'Heat and temperature', at what temperature does ice melt? (0 °C.) Everything around you is matter: it has mass and takes up space. Matter comes in three states: solid, liquid and gas.
Solids keep their own shape and size: a stone, a spoon, a block of ice. You can hold them. Some can be squashed or bent, but they do not flow. Sand pours, but each grain is a tiny solid.
Liquids flow and take the shape of their container, but the amount (the volume) stays the same: pour 1 litre of juice into any jug and it is still 1 litre. The top of a liquid stays flat and level.
Gases spread out to fill all the space they are in, and they can be squashed into a smaller space. Air is a mix of gases. Water as a gas is called water vapour: you cannot see it.

Heating and cooling can change a state. Melting: a solid turns into a liquid. Freezing: a liquid turns into a solid. Ice melts and water freezes at the same temperature, 0 °C. Iron melts only at 1,538 °C.

Water boils at 100 °C: bubbles of water vapour form all through it. It also evaporates from its surface far below boiling: puddles dry up and washing dries, faster when it is warm, windy and spread out.

Condensing: when water vapour cools, it turns back into drops of liquid. That is why a cold can gets wet on the outside and a bathroom mirror mists up. Evaporation and condensation move water round the world.

Try it in the world: tap TRY IT IN THE LAB on this unit's page to melt ice, boil water and freeze it again. Then time an ice cube melting in a warm room. Next, in grade 5: matter is made of particles.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a liquid?
exercises.hint: Which one can you pour, and takes the shape of its cup?
exercises.explain: Milk flows and takes the shape of its container: a liquid.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a gas?
exercises.hint: A gas spreads out to fill its space.
exercises.explain: Air is a mix of gases, and it fills the balloon.

exercises.prompt: A solid keeps its own shape.
exercises.hint: Think of a stone in a cup.
exercises.explain: True: a solid keeps its shape; it does not flow to fill its container.

exercises.prompt: What is it called when ice turns into water?
exercises.hint: A solid is turning into a liquid.
exercises.explain: Melting: a solid (ice) turns into a liquid (water).

exercises.prompt: At what temperature does water freeze?
exercises.hint: It is the same temperature that ice melts at.
exercises.explain: Water freezes at 0 °C, the same temperature that ice melts at.

exercises.prompt: What state of matter is in the jar outlined in orange?
exercises.hint: Does it keep its shape, lie flat at the bottom, or fill the whole jar?
exercises.explain: It spreads out to fill the whole closed jar: a gas.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: solid, liquid or gas?
exercises.hint: Does it keep its shape, flow, or spread out to fill a space?
exercises.explain: Solids: the stone and ice. Liquids: honey and orange juice. Gases: water vapour and air.

exercises.prompt: Why does a puddle disappear on a sunny day?
exercises.hint: Where does the water go when it warms up?
exercises.explain: The Sun warms the water and it evaporates: it turns into water vapour in the air.
choices: The water evaporates into the air.

exercises.prompt: Drops form on the outside of a cold can of juice. Where does the water come from?
exercises.hint: What is in the air that could turn into drops when it cools?
exercises.explain: The air has water vapour in it. On the cold can it cools and condenses into drops.
choices: water vapour in the air, condensing

exercises.prompt: Match each change to what happens.
exercises.hint: Melting is what ice does in the sun.
exercises.explain: Melting: solid to liquid. Freezing: liquid to solid. Evaporating: liquid to gas. Condensing: gas to liquid.

exercises.prompt: Washing dries faster on a warm, windy day.
exercises.hint: What helps water evaporate?
exercises.explain: True: warmth and wind make water evaporate faster.

exercises.prompt: Tilly pours 1 litre of water from a tall jug into a wide bowl. How many litres are in the bowl?
exercises.hint: Does the amount of a liquid change when its shape does?
exercises.explain: Still 1 litre: a liquid takes the shape of its container, but its volume stays the same.

exercises.prompt: Water is boiling in a pan. What does the thermometer show, in °C?
exercises.hint: Read the number at the top of the red liquid.
exercises.explain: The thermometer shows 100 °C: water boils at 100 °C.

exercises.prompt: Sand can be poured. Is it a solid or a liquid?
exercises.hint: Look at one grain of sand. Does it keep its own shape?
exercises.explain: Sand is a solid: each grain keeps its own shape. It only pours because the grains are tiny.
choices: a solid: each grain keeps its shape
a gas, because it spreads out

exercises.prompt: Iron melts at 1,538 °C. What state is iron in at 1,000 °C?
exercises.hint: Is 1,000 °C above or below iron's melting point?
exercises.explain: 1,000 °C is below 1,538 °C, so the iron is still a solid.

exercises.prompt: Water only evaporates when it boils at 100 °C.
exercises.hint: Think of a puddle on a warm day.
exercises.explain: False: water evaporates from its surface far below boiling. That is how puddles dry up.

exercises.prompt: Put the water cycle in order, starting at the sea.
exercises.hint: Start with the Sun warming the sea, and end with the water back in the sea.
exercises.explain: Evaporation, rising and cooling, condensing into clouds, then rain back to the sea: the water cycle.
items: Rain falls and flows back to the sea.
The water vapour rises and cools.
The Sun warms the sea and water evaporates.
It condenses into drops that make clouds.

exercises.prompt: A bathroom mirror mists up after a hot bath. Which change of state is this?
exercises.hint: Warm water vapour meets the cold mirror.
exercises.explain: Water vapour from the bath cools on the mirror and condenses into tiny drops.

exercises.prompt: Chocolate melts in a warm hand, but a spoon does not. Why?
exercises.hint: Does everything melt at 0 °C?
exercises.explain: Every material has its own melting point. Chocolate melts a little below body temperature; steel only at well over 1,000 °C.

exercises.prompt: Sort the changes: does water need heating, or cooling?
exercises.hint: Solid to liquid to gas needs heat. Going back the other way needs cooling.
exercises.explain: Heating: melting, evaporating and boiling go from solid to liquid, or liquid to gas. Cooling: a misty mirror, freezing and raindrops in a cloud go from gas to liquid, or liquid to solid.
